mmhub.title: Everything becomes tokens / vectors
mmhub.body:
Whether text, images, sound or video, it all ends up as a sequence of vectors queued into the model.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Everything becomes tokens / vectors
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 There’s no dedicated simulation for this part yet; browse “All labs” on the “Reference” stop.

🎯 Role

  • Text is cut into tokens, images into small squares, sound into short clips, video into “space-time patches”, and each piece becomes a vector.
  • The model always faces “a sequence of vectors”.

🌱 Where it starts

Produced by each encoder.

🔧 How training adjusts it

No parameters involved.

▶ What it does in use

On every multimodal input.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

With a unified format, the same Transformer can handle every modality, and different modalities can “talk” directly inside attention.

✅ Why this works

Attention doesn’t care where a vector came from, only about relevance, so “the cat in the picture” and “the cat in the question” can be linked.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Information density differs a lot between modalities (one image may take hundreds or thousands of tokens), using up a lot of context.

vit.title: Vision encoder (ViT)
vit.body:
Cuts an image into small patches and processes them with a Transformer into a sequence of “visual tokens”.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Vision encoder (ViT)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • The image is cut into small squares of, say, 16×16 pixels
  • each is flattened and multiplied by a table to become a vector, position information is added, and then it passes through several Transformer layers.
  • The output is one vector per patch, already blended with the context of the whole image.

🌱 Where it starts

Often pretrained first with methods such as image–text contrastive learning.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Adjusted during pretraining; once attached to the LLM it is often frozen or lightly fine-tuned.

▶ What it does in use

Computed once per input image.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Turning an “image” into the same kind of sequence as “text” lets it reuse everything learned about Transformers.

✅ Why this works

Attention lets each patch see the whole image (“this patch is a cat’s ear because next to it is a cat’s face”); after training on large-scale data the features are very general.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Cutting into patches loses detail, so small text and dense tables are often a struggle; high-resolution images need many patches and are expensive (scaling or tiling strategies are common).

patch.title: Patches + patch embedding
patch.body:
Cuts the image into squares and turns each into a vector.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Patches + patch embedding
🔥 Partly learnable: only a small set of numbers is adjusted by training
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

A 16×16 colour patch has 16×16×3=768 numbers, multiplied by a learnable table to compress it into one vector. Number of patches = (width÷16) × (height÷16).

🌱 Where it starts

That table is randomly initialized.

🔧 How training adjusts it

The table is trained.

▶ What it does in use

Done once per image.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Just as text is cut into tokens, images need a “basic unit” too. Pixel by pixel is too long; patches are the right compromise.

✅ Why this works

Patches small enough keep local texture, without too many of them.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Patch size is a trade-off: small patches keep detail but mean more tokens and more computation.

audenc.title: Audio encoder
audenc.body:
Turns sound into a spectrogram, slices it, and processes it into a sequence of “audio tokens”.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Audio encoder
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • The waveform is first converted into a mel spectrogram (a “photo” of sound: time on the horizontal axis, frequency on the vertical), cut into short time slices, and passed through a convolutional or Transformer encoder that outputs a sequence of vectors.
  • A neural audio codec can also compress the waveform directly into discrete tokens.

🌱 Where it starts

Often pretrained on large amounts of “audio–text” paired data (e.g. a speech recognition task).

🔧 How training adjusts it

Adjusted during pretraining; once attached to the LLM it can be frozen or fine-tuned.

▶ What it does in use

Computed once per input speech clip.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

A raw waveform has tens of thousands of numbers per second — too long; a spectrogram is close to how the human ear perceives sound and is easier to handle once compressed.

✅ Why this works

Tasks like speech recognition force the encoder to extract features of “what was said and how”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Noisy environments, accents and dialects remain challenging; subtle information about tone and emotion may be lost.

mel.title: Mel spectrogram
mel.body:
Breaks a short stretch of sound down into “which frequencies it’s made of”, laid out over time.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Mel spectrogram
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

Like a photo of sound: time on the horizontal axis, frequency on the vertical (compressed the way the ear perceives it), with colour intensity showing strength.

🌱 Where it starts

A fixed mathematical transform (Fourier transform + mel scale) with no parameters.

🔧 How training adjusts it

No parameters involved.

▶ What it does in use

Computed once per audio clip.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The human ear does a similar frequency breakdown itself; pitch and timbre are obvious at a glance on a spectrogram.

✅ Why this works

More compact than a waveform, with clearer patterns that are easier for a network to learn.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Phase information is discarded, so a vocoder has to “fill it back in” when turning it back into a waveform.

clip.title: Contrastive alignment (the CLIP idea)
clip.body:
Pulls the vectors of matching “image” and “text” pairs together and pushes non-matching ones apart.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Contrastive alignment (the CLIP idea)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Take huge numbers of “image–caption” pairs
  • a batch has N images and N sentences.
  • The image encoder and text encoder each produce vectors, and the similarity of every image–text pair is computed
  • the training goal: each image is most similar to its own caption and dissimilar to the others.

🌱 Where it starts

Both encoders are randomly initialized (or start from pretrained models).

🔧 How training adjusts it

Both encoders are adjusted together.

▶ What it does in use

Once trained, it can search images by text, provide text conditioning for generative models, and serve as the vision encoder of multimodal LLMs.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

“Do these two match?” is far cheaper than “label exactly what this is”, and the internet naturally has huge numbers of image–text pairs.

✅ Why this works

The contrastive objective forces both modalities into the same coordinate system: the text vector for “ginger cat sleeping” lands near photos of a sleeping ginger cat.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Biases and wrong captions in the paired data get learned; it is often insensitive to details like counts and spatial relations.

txtenc.title: Text encoder
txtenc.body:
Turns a caption into a vector in the same space as the image vectors.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Text encoder
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

Usually a Transformer that reads a sentence and outputs one vector representing its whole meaning.

🌱 Where it starts

Randomly initialized or starting from a language model.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Adjusted during contrastive training.

▶ What it does in use

Searching images by text, or serving as the “text condition” for image generation.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

We need a text representation that can be compared with image vectors.

✅ Why this works

Trained together with the image encoder, so the coordinate systems are naturally aligned.

⚠️ Limits / notes: When a caption is too long or complex, one vector can’t hold every detail.

projector.title: Projector / adapter
projector.body:
“Translates” visual/audio vectors into the word-vector format the LLM can read.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Projector / adapter
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • The vectors from the encoder differ from the LLM’s word vectors in length and meaning.
  • A small network (one or two tables, or a small module with attention) maps them across, sometimes also compressing many patches into fewer tokens.

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Often trained alone first (with the encoder and LLM frozen), then fine-tuned together.

▶ What it does in use

Each image/audio clip passes through it once.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Lets an already strong vision encoder and an LLM “talk to each other” without training either from scratch.

✅ Why this works

Training just a small adapter connects the two sides, needing far less data and compute.

⚠️ Limits / notes: If the adapter’s capacity is limited, it becomes an information bottleneck.

mllm.title: Multimodal LLM
mllm.body:
Visual/audio tokens are lined up with text tokens and understood together by the LLM.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Multimodal LLM
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 There’s no dedicated simulation for this part yet; browse “All labs” on the “Reference” stop.

🎯 Role

  • The flow: image → vision encoder → projector → a sequence of “visual tokens”, concatenated with the text tokens of the question and fed into the LLM
  • the LLM reads them like text and answers “how many cats are in the picture”.
  • There is also a “natively multimodal” route that trains on mixed-modality data from the start.

🌱 Where it starts

The LLM part usually comes from a pretrained language model.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Fine-tuned on image–text dialogue data to learn to answer about images.

▶ What it does in use

Used when looking at images, listening to audio, or reading screenshots of documents.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Reuses a strong language model’s knowledge and reasoning, only teaching it to “read the new tokens”.

✅ Why this works

Attention lets the text question directly “look up” the relevant image patches.

⚠️ Limits / notes: It can still get details, counts and exact positions wrong; hallucinations (claiming something is in the picture that isn’t) still happen.

gtext.title: Text generation (autoregressive)
gtext.body:
Writes text token by token, like a word chain.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Text generation (autoregressive)
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 There’s no dedicated simulation for this part yet; browse “All labs” on the “Reference” stop.

🎯 Role

The standard way an LLM generates: compute probabilities → sample → append → compute again.

🌱 Where it starts

See LLM.

🔧 How training adjusts it

See LLM training.

▶ What it does in use

Every answer is written this way.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Any text can be broken into a sequence of “next word” choices.

✅ Why this works

Each step sees the whole preceding text, so the result is coherent.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Once a step goes astray, the rest follows the error; generating one at a time, long answers take time.

gimg.title: Image generation (diffusion)
gimg.body:
Starting from a cloud of noise, “sculpts” an image step by step under the guidance of text.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Image generation (diffusion)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • In training it learns to “remove a little noise from a noised image”
  • in generation it starts from pure noise and denoises repeatedly for dozens of steps (speed-up methods need as few as a handful), usually in a compressed latent space, and finally decodes to pixels.

🌱 Where it starts

The denoising network is randomly initialized; the latent autoencoder is usually trained beforehand.

🔧 How training adjusts it

The denoising network learns to predict the noise.

▶ What it does in use

Every generation starts from fresh random noise, so every image is different.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

“Drawing a good picture out of nothing” is hard; “making a blurry picture a bit clearer” is easy. Split it into many small steps, each simple.

✅ Why this works

From huge numbers of images the denoising network has learned “roughly what real images look like”, and every step pushes a little towards “more like a real image, more in line with the text”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Fingers, text rendering, counts and spatial relations often go wrong (varies by model); there are also other routes, such as autoregressive and hybrid ones.

denoise.title: Denoising network
denoise.body:
Looks at the noisy image, the time step and the text condition, and predicts “what the noise is”.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Denoising network
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Common architectures are the U-Net or a diffusion Transformer.
  • Input: noisy latent + current step + text vector
  • output: an estimate of the noise
  • subtracting part of it gives a clearer image.

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Loss = the gap between predicted and true noise, adjusted over and over.

▶ What it does in use

Called dozens of times (or fewer) per generated image.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

A simple objective (error in predicting noise), with stable training.

✅ Why this works

Each step does just one small thing, so errors don’t easily spiral.

⚠️ Limits / notes: It needs many calls, so generation is slower than producing an image in one shot.

vae.title: Latent autoencoder
vae.body:
First compresses the image into a much smaller “latent space”, diffuses there, and finally decompresses back to pixels.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Latent autoencoder
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

The encoder compresses a 512×512 image into, say, several 64×64 channels; the decoder restores it in reverse. Diffusing on the small image is far cheaper.

🌱 Where it starts

Trained separately first.

🔧 How training adjusts it

The training goal is “compress, then restore faithfully”.

▶ What it does in use

During generation only the decoder is used, to turn the result back into pixels.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Denoising directly on millions of pixels is too expensive, and most pixel-level detail can be left to the decoder.

✅ Why this works

The latent space keeps semantics and structure, so diffusion only needs to focus on “what to draw”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Compression loses detail; small text and complex textures may be distorted.

tcond.title: Text conditioning + guidance
tcond.body:
Turns the prompt into vectors injected into the denoising network; the guidance strength decides how “obedient” it is.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Text conditioning + guidance
🔥 Partly learnable: only a small set of numbers is adjusted by training
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • A text encoder turns the prompt into vectors that tell the denoising network “which way to denoise” through cross-attention.
  • “Classifier-free guidance” is common: compute both the conditioned and unconditioned predictions and amplify the difference by some factor.

🌱 Where it starts

The text encoder usually comes from a pretrained model.

🔧 How training adjusts it

The denoising network learns to use the text condition; conditions are randomly dropped during training so it can also make unconditioned predictions.

▶ What it does in use

The guidance factor is set by the user or the system.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Without a condition, the model just draws “some decent-looking image”.

✅ Why this works

Amplifying the “conditioned − unconditioned” difference amounts to emphasizing “the part related to the text”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Too large a factor makes colours oversaturated, the image stiff, and variety lower.

gaud.title: Audio generation
gaud.body:
Turns sound into “acoustic tokens” or a spectrogram, generates it autoregressively or by diffusion, then restores the waveform.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Audio generation
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Speech synthesis: text → acoustic model (decides timbre, intonation, pauses) → acoustic tokens or spectrogram → decoder/vocoder → waveform.
  • Music generation works similarly but has to handle melody, harmony, rhythm and longer structure.

🌱 Where it starts

Each component is trained separately.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Trained on large amounts of “text–speech” or “description–music” data.

▶ What it does in use

When you ask it to “read this aloud” or “generate some music”.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Waveforms are too long; compress them into compact tokens first, and methods that matured on text (Transformers, autoregression) can be carried over directly.

✅ Why this works

The codec compresses one second into tens to hundreds of tokens that the model can easily handle; the vocoder restores the details.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Voice cloning can be abused for impersonation scams, so legitimate products need authorization and watermarks; structural consistency in long music remains hard.

codec.title: Acoustic tokens (neural audio codec)
codec.body:
Compresses a waveform into a sequence of discrete tokens that can be decoded back.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Acoustic tokens (neural audio codec)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 There’s no dedicated simulation for this part yet; browse “All labs” on the “Reference” stop.

🎯 Role

Multi-level “residual vector quantization” is common: the first level captures the gist, later levels add detail step by step.

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Training goal: after compressing and restoring, it should sound as close to the original as possible.

▶ What it does in use

During generation the tokens written by the model are decoded into sound.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Turning sound into “IDs in a vocabulary” too lets a language model “write sound” the way it writes text.

✅ Why this works

Coarse-to-fine levels make it compact while keeping audio quality.

⚠️ Limits / notes: The harder it compresses, the worse the audio; more levels mean more tokens and slower generation.

acoustic.title: Acoustic model / audio language model
acoustic.body:
Writes acoustic tokens or a spectrogram from text (and a reference voice).

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Acoustic model / audio language model
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 There’s no dedicated simulation for this part yet; browse “All labs” on the “Reference” stop.

🎯 Role

It can be an autoregressive “audio language model” writing tokens one by one, or a diffusion/flow-matching style method generating a spectrogram or continuous representation.

🌱 Where it starts

Randomly initialized or starting from a language model.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Trained on large amounts of paired data.

▶ What it does in use

Runs every time speech is synthesized.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Turns “what to say” into “how to say it”: intonation, pauses, timbre.

✅ Why this works

Large-scale data teaches it natural prosody; given a short reference clip it can imitate a voice (use only with authorization).

⚠️ Limits / notes: Fine control of emotion and prosody is still imperfect.

vocoder.title: Vocoder / decoder
vocoder.body:
Turns a spectrogram or acoustic tokens back into a playable waveform.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Vocoder / decoder
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 There’s no dedicated simulation for this part yet; browse “All labs” on the “Reference” stop.

🎯 Role

The spectrogram has lost the phase; the vocoder uses a neural network to “fill the details back in”, outputting tens of thousands of samples per second.

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Training goal: the restored waveform sounds just like a real recording.

▶ What it does in use

The last step of every synthesis.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Turns “a photo of sound” back into “the sound itself”.

✅ Why this works

The neural network has learned the regularities of waveform detail from huge numbers of recordings.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Quality and speed have to be balanced; audio quality differs noticeably between vocoders.

gvid.title: Video generation
gvid.body:
Diffuses in a “spatio-temporal latent space” so every frame looks good and consecutive frames are coherent.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Video generation
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

The video is compressed into spatio-temporal latents, cut into “space-time patches”, and a diffusion Transformer denoises all frames together starting from noise, finally decoding them into frames.

🌱 Where it starts

Components are randomly initialized or extended from image models.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Trained on large amounts of video (and image) data.

▶ What it does in use

Generates short videos from text or a first-frame image.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Video = images + time. To be coherent, all frames must be “considered together”.

✅ Why this works

Cross-frame attention keeps the same object consistent across frames; the bigger the scale, the better the image quality and coherence (an empirical trend).

⚠️ Limits / notes: Physics often goes wrong (objects passing through each other, things appearing from nowhere); the longer the video, the harder it is to stay consistent; computation is extremely expensive.

stlatent.title: Spatio-temporal latent
stlatent.body:
Compresses video along width, height and time at once.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Spatio-temporal latent
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Most of the content of adjacent frames is the same, so the time direction can be compressed a lot
  • after compression it is cut into cubes of “a few frames × a small region”, one token per cube.

🌱 Where it starts

The video autoencoder is trained separately.

🔧 How training adjusts it

The training goal is compress-then-restore faithfully.

▶ What it does in use

Encoding/decoding before and after generation.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Raw video is too much data to compute with uncompressed.

✅ Why this works

Keeps motion and structure while removing redundancy.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Fast motion and fine textures may be distorted.

dit.title: Diffusion Transformer (cross-frame attention)
dit.body:
Uses a Transformer as the denoising network so every space-time patch can “attend to” other frames.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Diffusion Transformer (cross-frame attention)
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

Denoises step by step just like image diffusion, but the network is a Transformer: the face patch in frame 1 can look directly at the face patch in frame 30.

🌱 Where it starts

Random initialization.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Predicts noise and is adjusted repeatedly.

▶ What it does in use

Called over many steps during generation.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Attention naturally spans both time and space.

✅ Why this works

All frames of the same object are processed together, so they naturally tend to be consistent.

⚠️ Limits / notes: The token count is huge, and computation grows fast with duration.

tempcons.title: Temporal consistency
tempcons.body:
The same thing must look the same across frames and move plausibly.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Temporal consistency
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

If each frame is generated separately, clothing colours and faces change from frame to frame (flicker). Joint denoising + cross-frame attention is the key to consistency.

🌱 Where it starts

A goal rather than a component.

🔧 How training adjusts it

The training data itself is coherent video, so the model is forced to learn coherence.

▶ What it does in use

An important criterion for judging video quality.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The human eye is extremely sensitive to flicker and sudden changes.

✅ Why this works

A shared context lets the frames be generated “in consultation” with each other.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Long videos and complex motion still drift.

g3d.title: 3D generation
g3d.body:
First choose a 3D representation, then “sculpt” a solid object with the help of 2D generation abilities or 3D data.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › 3D generation
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Common routes: ① multi-view diffusion first generates several views of the same object, then a reconstruction model assembles them into 3D
  • ② score distillation: use a 2D image model as a “judge” to optimize the 3D repeatedly
  • ③ train a generative model directly on a 3D representation.

🌱 Where it starts

Depends on the route.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Depends on the route.

▶ What it does in use

Input text or an image, output a 3D model.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

An object being plausible in 3D ≈ looking plausible from every angle; there are far more 2D images than 3D data, so 2D knowledge can be borrowed.

✅ Why this works

Differentiable rendering makes “3D parameters → image” differentiable, so image-level signals can optimize the 3D.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Views may be inconsistent (the “multi-face problem”); the resulting meshes and textures often aren’t production-ready; the routes change fast.

rep3d.title: 3D representations: mesh / point cloud / NeRF / 3D Gaussians
rep3d.body:
What format describes a solid object.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › 3D representations: mesh / point cloud / NeRF / 3D Gaussians
🔥 Partly learnable: only a small set of numbers is adjusted by training
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Mesh: a surface made of triangles, the industry standard
  • point cloud: a pile of points with coordinates
  • NeRF: a neural network that takes a position and direction and outputs colour and density
  • 3D Gaussians: thousands of semi-transparent little ellipsoids that render very fast.

🌱 Where it starts

Depends on the representation (the parameters of NeRF/3D Gaussians start random or from a rough shape).

🔧 How training adjusts it

The parameters of NeRF and 3D Gaussians are optimized by “comparing renders with target images”.

▶ What it does in use

Used for rendering, editing, and exporting to games or film.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Each representation has its strengths and weaknesses in quality, speed and editability.

✅ Why this works

Differentiable representations (NeRF, 3D Gaussians) can be optimized directly with gradients.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Converting between them loses quality; generated results often need manual touch-up.

mview.title: Multi-view diffusion
mview.body:
Generates several consistent views of the same object in one go.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Multi-view diffusion
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

Trained on top of an image diffusion model so that it outputs front, back, left, right and other views at once, consistent with each other.

🌱 Where it starts

Usually starts from an image diffusion model.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Trained on multi-view images rendered from 3D data.

▶ What it does in use

The first step of 3D generation.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Turning “generate 3D” into “generate a few consistent images” makes it easier.

✅ Why this works

It borrows a great deal of knowledge from image models.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Views may still not be fully consistent.

recon.title: 3D reconstruction
recon.body:
Assembles a 3D model from several view images.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › 3D reconstruction
🔥 Has learnable parameters: adjusted in training, read-only in use
🧪 There’s no dedicated simulation for this part yet; browse “All labs” on the “Reference” stop.

🎯 Role

It can optimize a NeRF/3D Gaussians object by object, or a trained feed-forward model can output 3D directly, which is much faster.

🌱 Where it starts

Depends on the method.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Feed-forward reconstruction models are trained on large amounts of 3D data.

▶ What it does in use

After multi-view generation.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Information from several angles is enough to constrain a solid shape.

✅ Why this works

The more views and the more consistent they are, the more accurate the reconstruction.

⚠️ Limits / notes: With few or inconsistent views, holes and artefacts appear.

sds.title: Score distillation
sds.body:
Uses a 2D image diffusion model as a “judge” to make a 3D object “look right” step by step.

📍 Location: App overview › Multimodal › Score distillation
⚙️ No learnable parameters: a fixed program / fixed rule / value computed on the fly
🧪 There’s no dedicated simulation for this part yet; browse “All labs” on the “Reference” stop.

🎯 Role

  • Render the current 3D from a random angle → add noise → let the 2D model denoise according to the prompt → update the 3D parameters in the direction of “how it wants to change it”.
  • Repeat many times.

🌱 Where it starts

The 2D model isn’t trained; what’s optimized are the parameters of the 3D representation.

🔧 How training adjusts it

Each object is optimized separately, which is slow.

▶ What it does in use

A representative idea of early text-to-3D.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Needs no 3D training data.

✅ Why this works

The 2D model knows “roughly what things look like from each angle”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Slow; prone to the “multi-face problem” and oversaturated colours.
